summary: Discusses how to protect block storage protocols running over IP using IPsec and IKE. It develops threat models and security approaches for iSCSI, iFCP and FCIP, plus the iSNS and SLPv2 discovery protocols, and looks at performance and resource limits. It was updated by RFC 7146.

plainLanguage.summary: Storage protocols can send disk commands and data across IP networks, where other parties may be able to interfere. This RFC explains how IPsec and IKE protect that traffic and the discovery information used to find storage devices.

subtitle: Security requirements for storage and discovery protocols that carry block data over IP.

tldr.problem: iSCSI, iFCP, and FCIP carry storage commands or data over IP, where packets can be read, changed, injected, or replayed. The storage protocols cannot rely on the physical protections assumed by SCSI and Fibre Channel.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies IPsec ESP for per-packet protection and IKE for authentication and key management, with required algorithms and operating rules. It also covers iSCSI login authentication and protection for iSNS and SLPv2 discovery.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records requirements also included in the iSCSI, iFCP, and FCIP specifications; those protocol documents take precedence if they differ. RFC 3723 was updated by RFC 7146.

today: RFC 3723 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7146. Its text says that the individual iSCSI, iFCP, and FCIP standards take precedence if their requirements differ.

sections.title: Storage Protocols That Use IP
sections.content:
This RFC covers three block storage protocols that use the Internet Protocol (IP): iSCSI, which carries Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) commands over the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP); iFCP, which connects Fibre Channel devices through gateways over TCP/IP; and FCIP, which carries Fibre Channel frames over TCP/IP. It also addresses the Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS) and Service Location Protocol version 2 (SLPv2) discovery protocols.

These protocols do not provide their own complete per-packet protection. The RFC uses IP security (IPsec) to protect IP traffic and the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) to authenticate peers, negotiate security associations, and manage keys. The requirements here apply to IP storage use, not to every IPsec implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: These protocols let computers access storage across an IP network. The RFC specifies how to protect their packets and how to secure the discovery services that help devices find one another.

sections.title: Threats and Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists threats to both control and data packets: snooping, modification, injection, connection hijacking, denial of service, impersonation, and attacks on discovery. A successful attack against an iFCP or FCIP gateway could affect the Fibre Channel hosts behind it.

The security protocols must support per-packet confidentiality, origin authentication, integrity, and replay protection, along with perfect forward secrecy during rekeying. They must provide mutual endpoint authentication. Security is mandatory to implement but not mandatory to use; configuration and policy determine which services are enabled.

The design also considers implementation resources. It says an implementation should be feasible at 1 Gbps, with 10 Gbps highly desirable, and discusses code-size constraints for embedded host bus adapters.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker could read or alter storage traffic, pretend to be a storage peer, or disrupt discovery. Implementations must support packet protection and mutual authentication, while operators choose services through policy.

sections.title: IPsec and IKE Requirements
sections.content:
Conforming implementations must support the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) for control and data packets, with per-packet authentication, integrity, and replay protection. They must support 3DES in CBC mode for confidentiality and HMAC-SHA1 for authentication and integrity. AES in Counter mode and AES CBC-MAC with XCBC are recommended options; ESP with NULL encryption must be supported for authentication without encryption. DES in CBC mode should not be used.

ESP tunnel mode is required; transport mode is optional. IKE is required for peer authentication, security association negotiation, and key management. Manual keying is prohibited because it does not provide the needed rekeying support. Implementations must support pre-shared-key authentication and IKE Main Mode; certificate authentication is optional and Aggressive Mode is recommended.

The RFC advises offering 3DES-CBC with HMAC-SHA1 for interoperability. When Diffie-Hellman groups are offered, it recommends at least 1024 bits for that pair, and at least 2048 bits when AES-CTR with XCBC-MAC is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices need a shared set of IPsec and IKE features so they can protect packets and agree on keys. The RFC requires certain algorithms and rejects manually configured keys because they cannot support rekeying.

sections.title: iSCSI Login Authentication
sections.content:
iSCSI login can authenticate initiators and targets when a connection starts, but it does not protect each packet or provide confidentiality, integrity, or replay protection. The RFC therefore treats login authentication alone as insufficient.

Compliant iSCSI implementations must support bidirectional CHAP authentication. They must support randomly generated secrets up to 128 bits, and must not offer non-random secret generation. If a CHAP secret is shorter than 96 bits, IPsec encryption must protect the connection, and login must not continue unless the implementation can verify that protection.

The RFC also requires separate secrets for the two authentication directions and warns against reusing a secret across multiple initiators or targets. Implementations may support SRP; targets must offer the SRP-1536 group.
sections.plainLanguage: iSCSI login checks identities at connection setup, while IPsec protects the packets that follow. The RFC sets rules for strong random CHAP secrets and requires encryption when a secret is shorter than the stated threshold.

sections.title: Protecting Discovery and Policy
sections.content:
iSCSI and FCIP can use SLPv2 to discover peers; iFCP requires iSNS, and iSCSI may use it. Discovery can also distribute security policy. If a device already obtained that policy another way, it must not request the same information through discovery.

When discovery distributes policy, it must receive packet authentication, integrity, and replay protection. For iSNS policy distribution, authentication, integrity, and confidentiality must protect all messages. The RFC recommends IPsec ESP with a non-null transform for unicast SLPv2 messages; multicast requests remain unprotected, so a user agent must verify that a reply answers a request it actually sent.

The RFC notes that SLPv2's own security does not provide confidentiality and cannot authenticate zero-result replies. It also discusses protecting iSNS heartbeat messages and using a negative cache when authentication fails.
sections.plainLanguage: Discovery can reveal storage devices and can distribute rules about how to secure them. When those rules travel through discovery, the discovery messages need protection too.

sections.title: Storage Connections and Security Associations
sections.content:
An iSCSI session can contain several TCP connections. Each connection is protected by one IKE Phase 2 security association, although one association may protect multiple connections. The initiator and target complete IKE before the initiator contacts the target on TCP port 3260.

An IKE Phase 2 delete message does not mean the storage connection has ended. iSCSI uses its Logout command for graceful teardown; if a security association is removed while a connection remains open, a new association can protect later traffic. iFCP and FCIP gateways require mutual authentication. For FCIP, the security association is established before the TCP connection begins.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec security associations protect storage connections, but their lifetimes are not the same as the storage session's lifetime. Removing an idle association does not by itself close the storage connection.

sections.title: Tunnel Mode, Transport Mode, and NAT
sections.content:
Tunnel mode adds an outer IP header, which reduces the path MTU and can reduce the maximum TCP segment size. It uses inner and outer addresses. It can also let a firewall terminate and inspect a tunnel while the storage endpoints keep communicating end to end. Transport mode keeps IPsec and the application on the same host and can allow closer integration.

Tunnel-mode ESP can cross a NAT in limited circumstances. TCP carried within transport-mode ESP cannot normally cross a NAT because the TCP checksum includes IP address fields and the ESP integrity check protects that checksum. The RFC points to IPsec and IKE NAT traversal, which can negotiate UDP encapsulation when a NAT is detected.

The RFC also warns that large IKE certificate exchanges may be fragmented and that some routers, NATs, and firewalls drop fragments. Path MTU discovery can also fail if unauthenticated ICMP messages are discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnel mode adds an outer packet header and may reduce the space available for data. NATs can also interfere with protected TCP traffic, so the RFC describes a separate NAT-traversal method.

sections.title: Rekeying, Throughput, and iSCSI Checksums
sections.content:
At high data rates, a 32-bit IPsec sequence number can be exhausted quickly. The RFC calculates that at 1 Gbps with 64-octet packets, this takes 2200 seconds. It also says that 3DES's 64-bit block size requires rekeying before 2^35 bytes, corresponding to 274.9 seconds at 1 Gbps and 27.5 seconds at 10 Gbps. Counter mode does not have this CBC block limit.

iSCSI adds a 32-bit CRC because the TCP checksum may miss errors at high speed. IPsec integrity checks are stronger and can simplify or replace iSCSI CRC recovery when protection is end to end. The CRC can still detect errors in software stacks, proxies, gateways, or paths where IPsec is provided by an external device.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast links use sequence numbers and cryptographic keys quickly, so implementations must rekey in time. An iSCSI checksum may add useful error detection when IPsec does not cover every part of the processing path.
